lesson.title: RTS/CTS: Solving the Problem You Cannot See
lesson.summary: RTS/CTS is an optional Wi-Fi handshake that lets a sender reserve the airwaves before transmitting, specifically to prevent collisions caused by hidden nodes, devices that cannot hear each other even though both can reach the same access point.
lesson.body:
CSMA/CA, the collision avoidance approach underlying Wi-Fi, works by having a station listen to the channel and wait for it to be quiet before transmitting. That works well when every station can hear every other station, but wireless signals have limited range, and it is entirely possible for two client devices to both be within range of the same access point while being too far apart, or blocked by a wall, to hear each other directly. This is called the hidden node problem: each station listens, hears silence because it cannot detect the other station's transmission, concludes the channel is free, and transmits, and the two transmissions collide right at the access point where both signals actually meet.

RTS/CTS, Request to Send and Clear to Send, is an optional exchange designed specifically to prevent this. Before sending a data frame, a station transmits a short Request to Send frame to the access point, including how long the upcoming transmission will take. If the access point is ready to receive, it replies with a Clear to Send frame, echoing that same duration. Crucially, both the RTS and the CTS frames are short enough, and reach a wide enough radius, that other stations nearby, including ones that could not hear the original sender directly, are very likely to hear at least the CTS reply from the access point, since the AP is typically in range of everyone.

Any station that overhears either the RTS or the CTS frame reads the duration field and sets a local timer called the Network Allocation Vector, or NAV, deferring its own transmissions until that timer expires, even though it never directly heard the sender it is deferring for. This is the clever part: it turns a problem of stations that cannot hear each other into a solution that only requires everyone to hear the access point, which they already need to do to use the network at all.

Picture a large conference hall with one access point at the front and two attendees seated at opposite corners in the back, more than a hundred feet apart with hundreds of other bodies absorbing signal between them. Neither attendee's laptop can hear the other's transmissions, but both can reach the access point at the front. Without RTS/CTS, both laptops might sense a quiet channel at the same moment and transmit simultaneously, colliding at the access point and wasting both transmissions. With RTS/CTS enabled, the first laptop sends an RTS, the access point replies with a CTS heard by both laptops, and the second laptop, now aware the channel is reserved even though it never heard the first laptop's data at all, waits until the reserved duration passes before attempting to transmit.

RTS/CTS is not free: the extra frames add overhead and a small delay to every transmission, so it is typically configured to trigger only for frames above a certain size threshold, or left disabled entirely on networks where hidden nodes are not a real problem, such as a small home with one or two devices near a single access point. It remains one of the clearest illustrations of how Wi-Fi's design compensates for a physical medium that wired Ethernet never had to worry about: two senders that are each fully visible to the receiver while being completely invisible to each other.
